noteText: Is this reaching into undocumented things?
response:
Yes. _url, contextProvider and emulatorOrigin live on the SDK's concrete FunctionsService, not on the public Functions type, which only declares app, region and customDomain. They are the exact members httpsCallable reads to build the URL (region, custom domain, emulator) and the auth, App Check and messaging headers. This was decision 2 at the goals gate: the public alternative needs the app to inject its Auth and App Check instances and the emulator host and port, which is the per-app wiring the feature exists to remove, and it still cannot see the emulator origin. Two guards cover the risk. Access is duck-typed here, so a missing or wrong-typed member makes the caller report a version mismatch through onError instead of sending a wrong request. And createKeepaliveFunctionCaller.test.ts builds real Functions instances from the real firebase/functions module and asserts the URLs and headers, so a dependabot SDK bump that renames one of these fails in CI rather than in production. No code change. Say the word if you would rather take the public route and have the app inject the collaborators.
<<<turn>>>
Switched to the public route per your decision in chat. getFunctionsInternals.ts is deleted. The URL now comes from the public app.options.projectId, region and customDomain plus an explicit emulator { host, port } dependency (internal/getCallableUrl.ts), and the headers from injected auth (authStateReady, then currentUser.getIdToken) and appCheck (getToken from firebase/app-check) instances (internal/getTokenHeaders.ts). noteText:
Is this real? Is this a potential issue? Should it be an option? Is this just sending a call that may have been intended to have been authenticated unauethenticated?
<<<turn>>>
no
response: Real, and yes it can send a call meant to be authenticated without the header. This branch runs when a user is signed in but getIdToken() rejects, which happens when the cached token has expired and the refresh fails (network down, refresh token revoked or the account disabled). It mirrors httpsCallable exactly. The SDK's context provider catches the same error and sends the request with no Authorization header, so the backend rejects it with unauthenticated. For httpsCallable that rejection reaches the caller as an error. Here it only reaches onError if the page is still alive, so the failure can vanish. Recommendation, no option needed. When auth was supplied and a user is signed in, a rejecting getIdToken() should not send. Report a KeepaliveCallError through onError with the auth error as cause and skip the fetch. The no-user case (currentUser null) stays a legitimate unauthenticated send, and App Check keeps its current behavior because the backend's unattested rejection is the intended signal there. This diverges from the SDK in one case where the SDK's behavior only makes sense because it can hand the rejection back. It changes approved requirement REQ-TOK-3 and one test. Want me to make that change?

noteText: Should we narrow this some more? Like only paid orders or is that too much?
response: Too much, unfortunately — the funnel reports Órdenes creadas and Órdenes pagadas as separate stages, so the drop-off between placing an order and the hold landing is exactly what this query has to show. Narrowing to paid would delete that stage. It is already range-bound, so it scales with the report window rather than with history.

noteText: This is not acceptable now or never.
response: Accepted — it has to go, and I want to get the replacement right rather than fast. What it feeds is customer history: new customers (first-EVER paid order falling in range), the 30-day repeat rate and median days to a second order, active customers, multi-business customers, and the journeys card. Everything there is windowed except one thing — deciding a customer is new needs to know they have no paid order before the range, which no range query can answer. Two ways to make it exact and bounded. (1) Fan out: query paid orders created in range (bounded), then for each distinct customer fetch their earliest two paid orders with limit(2) ordered by created. That answers new / repeat / median exactly, needs no schema change, and reads scale with range activity instead of lifetime volume. (2) Denormalise: add firstPaidOrderAt to CustomerSensitiveData, written when a customer's first order reaches succeeded, and query customers by it. Cheapest at read time, but it touches the payment write path and needs a backfill for existing orders. I would take (1) now and (2) later if read counts justify it. Say which and I will implement it; I did not want to reshape the metrics unilaterally when a subtle mistake changes numbers silently.

noteText: Why this unbounded search? Do we really need it?
response: Two of its three callers only needed a yes/no, so they now have bounded queries instead: locatedForCustomerQuery and anyForCustomerQuery, both limit(1).select(), fetching ids alone. forCustomerQuery survives for the one caller that genuinely needs a customer's full history — the report's journeys card, which counts how many known-source touches preceded a customer's first paid order. That is bounded by one customer's contacts rather than by collection size, and it only runs for customers who converted in the range.

noteText: This getting ALL of the customers touches makes no sense. It is so wasteful. Bad practice.
response: Agreed — fixed. It was reading a customer's entire touch history to answer two questions, both of which are now bounded: 'does any touch already have a restaurant' is a limit(1).select() existence check, and 'which touch is latest' reuses latestForCustomerQuery, which was already limit(1) and ordered. Three small reads instead of an unbounded one, and the in-memory reduce to find the newest touch is gone since Firestore already orders it.

noteText: This doesn't make sense.
response: You're right that it is wrong, and I want to name the actual defect rather than defend the intent. The intent was: if a link already told us the restaurant, the customer never chose one, so there is nothing to record. But the check asks 'does ANY touch have a location', which also swallows a real case — someone who arrived for restaurant A through a QR and then switches to restaurant B in the chat HAS chosen, and we record nothing. Their touch keeps saying A. So the guard conflates 'we already know a restaurant' with 'no choice was made'. The fix depends on the model question in the sibling note, so I have left the semantics alone (only made the read bounded) rather than change report numbers twice.

noteText: Why are the touch and the "resolved to a location" mixed in the touch itself? It is confusing.
response: It is confusing, and the confusion is real rather than cosmetic: the touch carries two unrelated facts. Where someone came from (source, label, timestamp) is an arrival — immutable, true forever. Which restaurant they ended up with (businessId, orderLocationId, resolvedAt) is a conversation outcome that can arrive later and change. Merging them is what forces this file to exist at all: read the history, decide whether a location is already there, mutate the newest arrival in place, or synthesise a fake arrival when there is none. That is also why the entity doc says touches are append-only while this code updates them. The cleaner model is to keep the touch as a pure arrival and store the restaurant selection once per customer — a small field on CustomerSensitiveData, which the webhook already has loaded. That deletes this whole file, makes touches genuinely immutable, and turns the sibling note's broken guard into a field check. The cost is real: the funnel's link-vs-generic split and the report's business scoping both read location off touches today, so both change, plus the backfill. I have not started it — it changes report numbers and is a bigger piece than a review fix. Worth doing before this ships, or worth a follow-up task; tell me which and I will do it.

noteText: Why is this necessary? Is it expected in modern browsers that we support?
response: Yes — needed in all modern browsers. The whole card is the click target (role=button + @click), and browsers fire a click when a select-drag starts and ends inside the same element. Without this guard, finishing a hand selection would trigger a copy + snackbar — which specifically breaks the copy-failure recovery flow, where the snackbar tells the user to select the code manually (REQ-COPY-5 mandates the suppression). CopyableUrl gets away without it because nobody hand-selects a short URL from a card that copies on tap; selecting code is an expected gesture here.

noteText: This seems to just silently fail. Is that expected?
response: Intentional, and specified: REQ-COPY-5 says no copy AND no snackbar when a selection sits inside the card — the selection itself is the feedback. The user just deliberately highlighted text; popping any message over that would be noise, and copying would overwrite the clipboard mid-manual-copy. It is a silent no-op, not a silent failure: nothing the user asked for was skipped.

noteText:
Is this a raw number? Give me a short brief with examples about this metric.
<<<turn>>>
So when sum happens it will still be accurate as, for every customer this happens at most once?
response:
A count per period, not a rate: how many customers made their first-ever payment at a second distinct business in that period. A customer is counted at most once in their lifetime — the "crossing" is the second business they ever paid at, read off the card's first-payment-per-business map.

Examples:
- Ana pays at Tacos Pepe in March (new customer in March) and at Burger Lab for the first time in May → May's figure +1, on the platform document and on Burger Lab's (the business the crossing landed on), not on Tacos Pepe's.
- Ana pays at a third restaurant in July → nothing; only the second business counts.
- Bob pays at Tacos Pepe five times → never counted.
- A business with one location can never see it on its own row; it only appears on the platform total and on the row of whichever business was somebody's second.

It sums across periods (one customer, one period) and exists only at document level (platform and per business), never per source. Rewrote the row to say it is a count, once per customer.
<<<turn>>>
Correction to the last bullet above: a business sees the figure on its own row only when it was the customer's second business; the first business never does.
<<<turn>>>
Yes. A customer crosses at most once in their lifetime and that crossing falls in exactly one period, so summing periods never counts anyone twice. The per-business rows are consistent with the platform figure for the same reason: each crossing lands on exactly one business (the second one), so the business rows add up to the platform total. The only way a past figure moves is a re-summarization after an order record changed, which is true of every derived number.

noteText: Is this always the same as location-resolved? or can it happen at different times?
response: Not always. `location-resolved` is a touch emitted when the conversation settles on a restaurant; `order-created` is derived from the order document's `created`. They coincide when `handleOrderInitiation` or a repeat creates a new order (same message, same instant). They differ when the customer already has an active order at that restaurant (resolved again, nothing created), when the capability menu or a handle link settles the restaurant before any order exists (resolved now, created later or never), and when a message continues an open order (neither). So "restaurants selected" counts distinct customers who settled in the period, "orders created" counts orders, and one customer can have several resolved touches per order, or an order whose resolved touch fell in the previous period.

noteText: Just curious. Do not make any changes, just discuss concisely. If in the future we decided to use unique codes from the browser that we wanted to pass through to the message to be able to link sessions, how complex would it be to incorporate? response: Moderate, and yes as an add-on. The code would ride in the CTA prefill phrase: `buildAttributionPhrase` / `parseAttributionPhrase` in `@okv/core` already carry a source and label through the message, so a device code is one more field, and the `contact` touch would then carry the device id. In the package, ownership only matters when a card is rebuilt (`readTouchesByOwner(customer)` plus the customer's orders), so linking means "also read the linked device's touches": a small link store plus one extra read in `rebuildOwnerCard`, behind a hook the host supplies. Nothing stored changes shape — touches keep their original owner, summaries are recomputed every run, cards are disposable — so one full re-summarization after the change applies the links to all history. What it does change is the model's "never linked" rule (the funnel break and the device-has-no-card assumption behind `CardlessOwnerKind`), so the doc and the funnel step would be reworded, and unlinked devices would remain the majority, since only arrivals through the phrase carry a code.

noteText: Does this mean that for any active order we read ALL of the orders the customer have ever placed? Every time they place an order?
response: Not per order, per run. Placing an order writes nothing here; the nightly run (and the Lab button) is the only reader. Each run rebuilds the card of every customer who has an event inside its window — normally the last 48 hours — and a card is built from that customer's whole history: their touches from the log and every order they ever placed, read through this hook in pages of 200. So a customer who ordered yesterday has all their orders read once tonight; a customer with no activity in the window is not read at all. Cost per run is roughly the order count of the customers active in the window. That is the price of cards being disposable (any card can be deleted and comes back identical); an incremental card would be cheaper to read and impossible to trust after a bug or an edited order.

This is odd. Do we really need this type? Is there a more idiomatic way to do this in TS?
<<<turn>>>
yes
response:
`(typeof List)[number]` is the standard TS idiom for "the type of a list's members", but it is odd here because the package already splits the vocabulary in two: `AttributionShape` has separate `touchType` and `derivedType` slots, and a config declares `touches` and `derived` separately. The idiomatic shape is two enums — `TouchAttributionEventType` (visit, qr-scan, whatsapp-click, contact, location-resolved, save-contact) and `DerivedAttributionEventType` (order-created, order-paid, order-captured, campaign-spend) — with `Object.values(...)` as the lists, so both `as const` arrays and both indexed types go away. Where code needs either, the package's `DeclaredEventType<OkvenAttributionShape>` is already that union. The browser subset stays a plain array of touch members with its indexed type, since a string enum cannot be a subset of another enum. Cost: every `AttributionEventType.X` use moves to one of the two enums (about 40 files; values unchanged, so snapshots do not move). I'd fold it into the rename pass with `contact` and `location-selected`. Go?
<<<turn>>>
Done. `AttributionEventType` is gone: `TouchAttributionEventType` and `DerivedAttributionEventType` are enums now, the lists are `Object.values(...)`, and both indexed types went away. The browser subset stays a plain array of touch members with its indexed type, since an enum cannot subset another enum. Call sites needing the union use `TouchAttributionEventType | DerivedAttributionEventType` (only `toAttributionEventId`).

noteText:
What is a "Report Note"? Do we have an existing or better concept name that is less ambiguous or more descriptive? Also are we using Kind interchangably with Type? In that case we should consolidate in a single name for a concept (settle on Type)
<<<turn>>>
1&2. settle on Type. Do we have a doc that tracks this type of decision?
3. is it needed? If so, wire it into the page. If the page is already deriving appropriately from the data, then drop it from the response.
response:
A report note is a caveat the engine attaches to a report response so the UI can flag a number to read with care: `preliminary` (repeat rate before the following month closes), `stale` (range reaches past `lastDataDay`), `sources-overlap` and `owners-per-period`. The package calls the type `ReportNote`; the design doc says "data-quality caveats". Two findings while checking: hosting never reads `notes` — the page derives its own wording from `lastDataDay` and the running period — so today the enum only travels on the wire; and yes, Kind and Type are mixed: `AttributionOwnerKind` and `AttributionReportNoteKind` here, and in the package `OwnerKind`, `MetricKind`, `CardedOwnerKind`, `EventOwner.kind`, `ReportNote.kind`.

Proposal: call the concept `ReportCaveat` ("note" also names the free-text notes on QR configs), discriminated by `type: ReportCaveatType`, owned by the package so the mirror goes (next note). Then settle on Type everywhere: `AttributionOwnerType`, `OwnerType`, `MetricType`, `owner.type`. The owner rename changes the stored log-line shape (`owner.kind` is a queried field) and touches about 80 files with snapshots; nothing is in production, so it is churn, not a migration.

Decisions I need: (1) `ReportCaveat` / `ReportCaveatType` ok, or another name? (2) Kind→Type everywhere including `owner.kind` in stored docs, or only the enum names? (3) Wire the caveats into the report page, or drop them from the response? I'll run it as one pass once answered.
<<<turn>>>
1&2: settled on Type and swept everywhere — `AttributionOwnerType`, `MetricType`, `CardedOwnerType`, `CardlessOwnerType`, `checkOwnerType`, and the stored `owner.kind` field is `owner.type` now (log lines, cards, every snapshot). The decision doc: CLAUDE.md's Code Style list is where these conventions live (naming.md only holds the function-verb table), and I recorded the rule there: classifying enums end in Type, never Kind, and the discriminator field is `type`. 3: not needed — the page never read `notes`; it derives staleness and the running period from `lastDataDay`/`runningPeriod`, preliminary from the lifecycle month, and the multi-period disclosure from the range itself. So the whole caveat surface is gone: package `ReportNote` type and its assembly, the wire `notes` field, the handler mapping, and the `AttributionReportNoteKind` mirror enum.

About the "unless the hold was released", does it get removed? Woudl it be worth keeping it? or perhaps replace with a `order-canceled`? Feels like a good metric to track? Explain the options. Customer paid is the action. Capture is when the transaction is finalized and then the accounting event happen. Be concise with your explanation.
response:
Nothing is removed: derived events are never stored, so on the next run a released-hold order simply yields `order-created` only and the paid count drops by one. The reason it works that way is the lifecycle rules: `order-paid` is the conversion event behind new / active / churned / repeat, so counting a released hold as "paid" would make a customer whose only order was rejected a new, active customer.

Agreed that "paid but lost, and why" is worth tracking. Options:
1. Keep `order-paid` as "money kept" and add derived `order-rejected`, `order-cancelled`, `order-expired` events at their status instants (all readable from `statusHistory`, nothing logged). Lost = the three counts; the reason comes free from the type. Recommended.
2. Make `order-paid` unconditional and add the loss events. The funnel paid → captured then shows the loss directly, but the lifecycle metrics pick up the false new customers above.
3. Leave as is.

Say which and I'll do it. Option 1 adds three derived types, a `toOrderEvents` branch, config declarations and report rows; the doc row here gets rewritten with it.
<<<turn>>>
Option 1 done: `order-rejected`, `order-cancelled` and `order-expired` are derived events now — a paid order whose hold was released yields its creation plus the loss event at the release instant (read from `statusHistory`; an unpaid cancel/expiry still yields creation only). Config declares them uncredited, the wire totals gained `ordersRejected/ordersCancelled/ordersExpired`, and the doc's event table and metrics row cover them. On active customers: I'd keep `order-paid`. With option 1, "paid" already means money kept — a released hold recounts the customer out — so the paid and captured cohorts differ only by orders still in flight and by boundary days. Paid is the customer's own act at their own instant; capture is fulfillment and can slip past a month boundary (paid Jan 31, picked up Feb 1 would move the activity into February). Say the word if you want it switched anyway — it is a one-line config change (`lifecycle.conversion`).
<<<turn>>>
(anchor correction — the loss mapping lives here)
<<<turn>>>
The two options for what "active customer" means:

**Paid (current):** active = the customer acted — committed money this month. A released hold recounts them out, so it is money kept, anchored to the customer's decision instant.

**Captured:** active = the transaction finalized — food handed over, money taken. Anchored to fulfillment, which can land a day (or month boundary) after the customer acted, and excludes paid orders still awaiting pickup at run time.

Exactly your framing: paid is the customer's action, capture is the accounting event. Lifecycle metrics ask "did this customer act this month," so I'd keep paid; the money metrics already count at capture, matching the financial report. One-line change (`lifecycle.conversion`) if you want captured instead.

noteText:
What does 'an owner active in two periods counts twice' mean?
<<<turn>>>
Does that mean that perhaps we should not show those values as they are misleading? 
<<<turn>>>
1
response:
It describes how a range total is built for metrics that count distinct owners: each period stores its own distinct count, and the range total is the sum of those, so one device that visited in both weeks of a two-week range contributes 1 to each week and 2 to the total. The engine cannot do better without owner ids in summaries. Rewrote the cell to say exactly that; it is also what the `owners-per-period` report note flags.
<<<turn>>>
They are not wrong, they are a different unit: for one period they are exact distinct counts; for a multi-period range they are "device-weeks" (or customer-months). Today the funnel, the source table and the business table show those sums for whatever range is picked, and the engine flags it with the `owners-per-period` note, which the handler forwards and the page ignores.

Options:
1. Say what the number is: when the range spans more than one period, label these columns as a sum of weekly (or monthly) uniques and render the caveat the engine already sends. Cheapest, and the funnel ratios stay meaningful since every stage is inflated the same way.
2. Show distinct-owner columns only for single-period ranges and dashes otherwise. Loses the source and business comparison over a month of weeks.
3. Make them exact: range-distinct counts need owner ids in every summary or a log scan at read time, both of which the design rules out (summaries hold no owner id; reports never scan the log). A package change and a storage cost.

I'd do 1. It is the same "wire the caveats into the page" decision as the report-note thread. Which one?
<<<turn>>>
Option 1 done, client-derived: `buildMultiPeriodNote` renders a footnote under the funnel card and the sources table whenever the range spans more than one period — "Este rango suma la gente de cada semana: quien vuelve en dos semanas cuenta dos veces." (month wording for month ranges), absent for a single period where counts are exact. Verified rendered in the dev emulator at 375px, both granularities; design review softened the original "los únicos" to "la gente". Since the fact is derivable from the requested range, the engine-sent caveat became unnecessary — it was removed with the rest of the notes surface (see the Report Note thread).

noteText: Do we have any rules for the use of the word `Derived` or similar?
response: No codified rule — naming.md only governs function verbs. "Derived" here comes from the design doc's own split of the event vocabulary: touches are logged the moment they happen, derived events are computed fresh from the orders and campaign-spend records on every run and never stored. The enum pair (`TouchAttributionEventType` / `DerivedAttributionEventType`) mirrors those two doc terms one-to-one, which I'd argue is the rule that matters: type names reuse the design doc's vocabulary instead of coining synonyms. If you want it written down, one line in CLAUDE.md's Code Style ("names reuse the design doc's vocabulary") would cover it — the existing "Reuse existing vocabulary" bullet already points that way for code terms.

Happy to add that casing rule as one line to packages/CLAUDE.md's constants section if you want it written down.

Yes. The repo does not enable noUncheckedIndexedAccess, so a plain Record<string, number> types card.firstAt['order-paid'] as number even when the key is missing. In the package's own types the keys are finite unions, where Partial is needed for a different reason: Record<DeclaredEventType, number> would require every event type present, so a card with no payment yet could not be typed. <<<turn>>>
Fair, and I tried it so I can point at the exact line. Keying firstAt by TouchAttributionEventType | DerivedAttributionEventType breaks one place: functions/src/utils/attribution/internal/createAttributionStore.ts, getCards (line 181), which returns the stored DBAttributionCard as the package's OwnerCard<S>. The reason is that the store is generic over the shape S. For an arbitrary S the compiler cannot prove Okven's event types cover DeclaredEventType<S>, whereas a string-keyed record satisfies any key union. So `string` here is not protecting any code, it is compensating for the adapter being generic when it is only ever built for Okven. That is the same finding as the proposal on attributionLog.ts:28: type the adapter on OkvenAttributionShape, and every one of these maps can be keyed by the real union. noteText: Should we be logging cancel or not?
response:
No, and nothing could be logged here even if we wanted to. The order being cancelled is unpaid (an empty shell the customer is walking away from to order elsewhere), and the design counts a cancel only when a paid order's hold is released, because those loss events say what money was lost and why. An unpaid cancel yields nothing past order-created, which stays counted: the customer did start an order. The loss events are also never written to the log; the nightly run derives them from the order's status and instants, so a diff at cancel time would show nothing either way. Only the location-selected touch for the new restaurant is stored, which is what the snapshot shows.

While here: three test comments still called the touch `location-resolved`, its old name, and the report handler's local constant did too. Renamed all four (1c22174a8); the Verify comment on this test now also says the cancel is not logged and why.

noteText: Are we showing these errors to the customer? Do we have a precedent where we create an enum so that we can show an appropriate error or are this things that the UX prevents to begin with?
response:
No, nobody sees these. Server-side, validateSchemaAndTrim turns a schema failure into a FunctionsInvalidArgumentError carrying this English text; client-side, createActionableFunctionCaller hands every non-connectivity failure to toActionableError, which raises a fatal error with the caller's own generic message, so staff get the error page and the schema text lives only in the cause and the function log. That is the same for every schema in packages/valid: the messages are for the developer reading logs, and they follow the siblings' register (getFinancialReportSchema: 'endDate must be on or after startDate').

The precedent for failures a user should read is the result enum: a handler returns one for an expected outcome (UpdateOrderStatusResult, RecordCampaignSpendResult, TrackAttributionEventResult.Skipped) and hosting maps it to Spanish. Schema rejections are treated as programming errors instead, and where a form can produce one, we run the same schema client-side first and map the ValidationError to copy, which is what useCampaignSpendForm does for the too-old date.

Here the UX makes all three unreachable. The page builds from, to and granularity from one place (getAttributionRange), so the keys are always spelled in the requested granularity. In the custom range the Desde list stops at the Hasta value and the Hasta list starts at the Desde value, so to is never before from. And the month list is cut to MaxSelectableMonths (59, with a comment naming this schema's cap), so the range can never reach 60 periods. The schema is the guard against a hand-built request, not a message path.

noteText: Should we create a schema for this and possibly others rather than repeating?
response:
Yes. Three field validators now live beside date() and currency() in packages/valid/src, each with its own test, and the four attribution schemas use them instead of spelling the rule inline (b0d53d11f):

- periodKey(): the week-or-month pattern that was here, used by from and to. WeekKeyPattern stays local, since only this schema's cross-field check (key spelled in the requested granularity) needs to tell the two apart.
- summaryGranularity(): `oneOf: Object.values(SummaryGranularity)`, which this schema and summarizeAttributionSchema's granularities array both had.
- attributionSource(): `oneOf: Object.values(AttributionSource)`, which recordCampaignSpendSchema and getCampaignSpendSchema both had.

Nothing else repeats across the five attribution schemas: trackAttributionEventSchema's device id, page and label rules each appear once. build-tsc, lint and the valid package's 339 tests pass; the schema tests did not change, since betterbe's messages are the same either way.

Yes, with one nuance per kind of number:

- Money and event counts (captured, orders created, paid, captured, rejected, spend) are the plain sum of the four months.
- People counts (visits, contacts, restaurants selected, save-contact taps, new customers) sum each month's distinct count, so a device or customer active in two of the months counts twice. - The Clientes card ignores the range and always shows the last closed month.

noteText: what is the difference between emit and track?
response: They differ by who does the writing. An emit* is the write itself, so it sits next to the log: the three emit* functions all call the engine's record through emitAttribution. A track* reports from where the thing happened to whatever keeps the record and does not wait on it, so the record can be a callable, a running tally or browser storage: the browser's trackAttributionEvent posts to the callable that then calls emitAttribution, trackFlaggedMessage appends to the decaying tally on the customer document, trackRecentQR writes localStorage. noteText: I thought the whole point of "batching" was to do it in different "awaits", is it not? Asking. No changes yet.
response:
A Firestore batch works the other way round. `batch.set` only queues a write in memory, and `batch.commit()` sends every queued write in one request and applies them all or none. So batching turns N awaited writes (N round trips) into one await per commit. `runBatch` from firebase-kit-admin is just create batch, run the callback, `await commit()`.

The awaits in this loop are per chunk because a single commit takes at most 500 writes (`FirestoreBatchLimit`). `toWriteChunks` splits the writes into chunks of that size, and each chunk is one atomic commit awaited in turn. A nightly run writes about 70 documents, so that is normally one commit.

Across chunks it is not atomic. If the second commit fails, the first chunk stays written. That is fine here, since every write is a whole-document overwrite and the run can be re-run. The chunks could commit in parallel with `Promise.all`, but at this volume one after another is simpler and keeps the write rate low. No change made.

response:
Numbered so you can pick.

1. **Level**: one block of numbers, with counts per event type, distinct owners, money and lifecycle metrics. A document has one for itself (`totals`) and one inside every row. It has four names:
   1.1 `SummaryLevel` in the package, the stored shape.
   1.2 `LevelBucket` in the package, the same numbers while a run is still adding them up, held as sets and maps.
   1.3 `AttributionDocumentLevel` in @okv/types.

2. **Row**: a level plus what it is keyed by. There are four kinds:
   2.1 Source row, keyed by source (`sources`).
   2.2 Label row, keyed by campaign label, inside a source row (`labels`).
   2.3 Acquisition row, a source row keyed by the customer's acquisition source (`acquisitions`).
   2.4 Group row, keyed by business, inside window and month documents (`groups`).
   The package calls them `SummarySourceRow`, `SummaryLabelRow` and `DocumentGroupRow`, two prefixes for one family. @okv/types repeats them as `AttributionDocumentSourceRow` and so on. Hosting's `SourceRow`, `SourceLabelRow`, `BusinessRow` and `CampaignRow` are dashboard view rows built from them.

**Vocabulary**

1. Event. One thing that happened to an owner at an instant, of a declared type.
   1.1 Touch. An event the host records as it happens. The log holds it.
   1.2 Derived event. An event the host reads back from its own data through hooks.
2. Owner. Who an event belongs to. Customer or browser.
3. Card. An owner's remembered first events and arrivals.
4. Arrival. A card's remembered visit, with source and label.
5. Credit. The source and label an event is attributed to.
6. Group. The host's grouping value (Okven's business). Overall. The roll-up across every group.
7. Totals. One block of numbers. Counts, owners, amounts, metrics.
8. Row. Totals keyed by one value. Source row, label row (inside a source row), group row.
9. Document. A stored summary. Day, window, month.
10. Bucket. The in-progress form of totals, a row or a document while a run builds it.
11. Range. A from and to pair of instants.
12. Span. A from and to pair of local days. A window is a span of fixed length at a position. A month is a span of one calendar month.
13. Rejection. Why a touch or derived event was refused.
14. Figures. The Dashboard's view of totals. Hosting only.

**How they combine**

- Stored shapes: `Document<Noun>`. `DocumentTotals`, `DocumentSourceRow`, `DocumentLabelRow`, `DocumentGroupRow`, `DayDocument`, `WindowDocument`, `MonthDocument`.
- Building: `<Noun>Bucket`. `TotalsBucket`, `RowBucket`, `DayBucket`.
- Time: `<X>Range` holds instants, `<X>Span` holds days.
- Verbs: `recordTouch`, `add<X>ToTotals`, `to<Noun>`, `build<Document>`.

**Collapses**

- level, summary, numbers → totals
- line, record (noun) → event
- records (hooks), derive → derived
- target, value, business, every → group, overall
- period → month
- window (as a read range) → range
- range (as days) → span

noteText: Should this throw? Or result in onError somehow?
response:
Neither, today. The skip is deliberate and only one thing reaches it. The log is append-only and keeps every touch ever recorded, so when a host stops declaring a type (this branch retired `qr-scan` in phase 1) the old rows stay. Every other path refuses an undeclared type up front: `recordTouch` rejects it before it is appended, and the derived-event hooks go through the same `validateEvent`, whose refusals land in `SummaryStats.rejectedEvents`. So by the time the day builder runs, an unknown type can only be a retired one.

Throwing would make every nightly run fail from the day a type is retired, with no way out short of rewriting the log. Options:

1. Keep the silent skip, as now.
2. Count skipped rows into `SummaryStats.rejectedEvents` with a `stale-type` reason, through the same `selectDistinctRejections` path the hooks use, so the Lab snackbar and the run log show "N touches of a retired type" instead of nothing. Never throw.
3. Add an `onStaleTouch` hook to the config so the host decides.

I recommend 2. It costs one reject reason and a few lines in `addEventToDayBuckets`, and it makes the retired rows visible where the run already reports refusals. Which do you want?

noteText:
what is this? Why not use the callable infrastructure/patterns we already have?
<<<turn>>>
this feels like we are reverse engineering the callable and could cause problems later. Am I wrong?
<<<turn>>>
give me a very brief brief for the fix to provide to the firebase-kit-client.

<<<turn>>>
A new version of firebase-kit-client was released. It should address this. Incorporate it.
response:
This is the browser posting the same request `fast.trackAttributionEvent` would send (the `{ data: { action, v, ...fields } }` envelope), by hand with `fetch`. It is deliberate, for two reasons I checked against the code:

1. `keepalive`. The WhatsApp CTA tap on the menu page navigates the tab to wa.me right away. A normal request is cancelled when the page unloads, and `fetch(..., { keepalive: true })` is what lets it finish. The shared caller goes through `createActionableFunctionCaller`, which calls the SDK's `httpsCallable(functions, name, { timeout })`. Neither exposes `keepalive` or a custom fetch, because the SDK's fetch hook is an internal constructor argument that `getFunctions` never takes. So with the shared caller, the tap that matters most would usually be lost. That is also why the App Check token is fetched before the call: nothing may wait on the network once the tap starts leaving.
2. Failure behaviour. Every `~/callables` group runs `checkRateLimit` and `withConnectivityHandling`. On a failed call, that raises the offline banner, refreshes the connection status, and rethrows as an actionable error. For an analytics ping on a public page, a blocked or offline request should do nothing visible, so this path swallows every failure instead.

The cost is that it rebuilds the URL itself: region, emulator port, envelope and App Check header, all of which the SDK normally owns.

Options:
1. Keep it as is. The reasons are in its doc comment.
2. Add a fire-and-forget mode to firebase-kit-client (your library), for example `createBeaconCaller`: `keepalive`, no connectivity or rate-limit wrapping, errors swallowed, URL and App Check handled there. This file would then call it like the other groups. That is a library change and release, so I would file it as Todoist "[infra] add a keepalive fire-and-forget caller to firebase-kit-client" and switch this file once it ships.

I recommend 2 with the Todoist item, keeping this file as is until then. Should I file it?
<<<turn>>>
Partly. Here is what it copies:
1. The request shape is not guessed. Firebase publishes the callable protocol, which covers the `{ data }` body, the `X-Firebase-AppCheck` header and the function URL formats. That part follows a documented contract.
2. What it copies by hand is our own setup, and that part can drift. `FunctionsRegion = 'us-central1'` and `FunctionsEmulatorPort = 5001` repeat values that live elsewhere, the SDK's default region and the port in firebase.json. If either moves, this call breaks.
3. It would also break silently. By design it swallows every failure, so a wrong URL would drop every visit and click with no error anywhere. Its test stubs `fetch`, so the test would not catch it either.

So yes, it can cause problems later, through 2 and 3.

Options:
1. A keepalive caller in firebase-kit-client (option 2 in my earlier reply). The protocol code lives once, in the library that owns it, and this file calls it like the other groups. It needs a library release and a Todoist item, which I would file only with your OK.
2. Keep the hand-built call, but log a failed response in development. A broken URL then shows up the first time the page loads locally, not months later in the numbers.
3. Use the normal `fast` caller and accept that a WhatsApp tap usually loses its click touch when the page leaves. The CTA phrase in the customer's first message still records the source they came from.

I recommend 1, with 2 applied now so a break is visible until the library ships. Which do you want?
<<<turn>>>
Brief for firebase-kit-client:

**Keepalive caller for callables**

Problem: when a tap sends the page away (for example a WhatsApp link), the browser cancels a callable request that is still in flight. `httpsCallable` offers no way to set `keepalive`, so apps end up building the callable request by hand, and that copy breaks silently if the region or emulator setup changes.

Ask: a fire-and-forget caller, for example `createKeepaliveCaller(functions, name)`, that:
1. Sends a callable protocol request with `fetch(..., { keepalive: true })`.
2. Builds the URL from the `Functions` instance the way `httpsCallable` does: region, custom domain, and emulator host and port.
3. Gets the App Check token, and the auth token when someone is signed in, before sending, since nothing can wait once the page starts to leave.
4. Skips connectivity handling and rate limiting, and never throws. Failures go to an optional `onError` callback.
5. Respects the `keepalive` body limit of 64 KB.

Okven would then replace the hand-built `fetch` in trackAttributionEvent.ts with this caller.
<<<turn>>>

noteText: Should it be 61? What happens for a 31 day month that follows a 30 day month?
response: Sixty is right, and month length does not enter into it. The two reads are independent and the earlier wins. Sixty days back serves the windows: the 30-day window and the 30-day window before it need exactly 60 whole days through last night, and the trailing start is computed as last night minus 59 days, so it is 60 days inclusive whatever the months are. The months are served by the other bound, the first day of the month before the last closed month, which is a date rather than a count, so a 31-day month after a 30-day one changes nothing.

noteText: is this the start of 12-31? shouldn't it be either the end of 12-31 or start of 1-1-2026?
response: It is the start of December 31, and that is right. The trailing read is 60 whole days through last night. Last night here is February 28, so the 60 days are December 31 through February 28 (1 + 31 + 28), and `from` is the first instant of the earliest one, midnight in Puerto Rico, which is 04:00Z. The end of December 31 or the start of January 1 would make it 59 days.

noteText: would this not have shown if the customer converted in May? Would this have received the right data where appropriate?
response:
Churn is measured against the month immediately before. `churned` in July is the count of customers who captured in June and not in July. A customer whose only capture was in May would count as churned in June's document, not July's, and July would read them as nothing (neither active nor churned) because a month only looks one month back.

That is the design's Dejaron de ordenar, "captured the month before, not this month", and it is why the nightly read reaches back to the first day of the month before the last closed month, so June's converters are known when July is built. A run that starts with data inside June (the partial month case) reports June's churn as unknowable rather than zero.

noteText: are we potentially reading orders 3 times from db?
response:
Three queries, but each order is read at most three times only when it was created, paid and captured inside the same range, and the `seen` set makes the second and third hits free of everything but the read. The reason there are three scans is that the three events hang on three different fields, `created` (an instant) and `paidDate` and `capturedDate` (local calendar days), and Firestore cannot range-filter one query on more than one field, so one scan per field is the only way to be sure no order the range owes an event is missed. Each scan is a paged, indexed range query, so the cost is proportional to the orders that fall in the range, not the collection.

What it does cost: an order that went created, paid and captured within the 60-day window is fetched three times per nightly run. At today's volume that is a few hundred document reads a night. If it ever matters, the cheap fix is to skip the `created` scan when `range.from` is before the oldest `paidDate` and rely on the other two, since a captured order was also created and paid; the honest fix is a single `attributionAt` field written on every status change so one scan covers all three. I would leave it until the read count shows up on the bill.

Where it matters: a partial month is left out of every series (12 meses, the six-month Clientes series) so no bar is silently short, and it is used for one thing only, the campaign lifetime sums on Campañas, where a partial start is still the truth. The design doc says so under Documents.
<<<turn>>>
Only the very first month can be partial. A month is partial when the data start (the day the log began) falls after its first day, and that is true of exactly one month ever, the one the log was switched on in. Every later month is whole by construction.

Why it is hidden from the series: the 12 meses and the six-month Clientes series were meant to compare like with like, and a first bar covering, say, nine days would read as a bad month rather than a short one. That is the whole reason the flag exists. It has two consumers, `selectClosedMonths` and one filter in `useDashboardPage`, both of which drop it.

If we remove the concept: the first month shows in every series with its true, short numbers, the last-closed-month comparison and churn can measure against it (fewer converters in a short month, so a smaller churn count, still the truth), and `partial` disappears from the document type, the month builder, the design doc, the two filters and their tests. Nothing else reads it. The cost is one honestly short bar at the start of the history, forever.

I recommend removing it. One fewer concept, and the short first month is a fact worth seeing rather than hiding. Say the word.
<<<turn>>>
Removed, commits 3daa4a0d3, 35b5729af, 3618a6e0f and their docs passes. `partial` is gone from the month document types, the month builder, the two Dashboard filters, 32 snapshot keys and two tests whose only subject it was. The first month with data now appears in every series with its true numbers, the design doc says so, and the nightly still skips a month that ended before the data start.

noteText:
Unrelated to this file. Would it eventually be possible to log an event for a customer using "lo de siempre" functionality to track that as past what makes people repeat? (Discuss only)
<<<turn>>>
would it be possible to answer something like... of customers that repeat, how many use lo de siempre? or other interesting questions? "lo de siempre" is only available after the first order is captured.
response:
Yes, and cheaply, because the pipeline already has a slot for it. Two ways:

1. A touch. The moment a customer accepts "lo de siempre", the webhook handler emits a `repeat-order-accepted` touch (customer owner, business dimension) exactly like `save-contact`. It shows up as a count and a distinct-customer figure on days, windows and months, and as a milestone in `lifecycle.milestones` it would tell you how many new customers had used it before their first capture, the same way saved contact does.
2. A derived event. If the order itself records that it came from a repeat (a flag on the order), the order hooks yield `order-captured-via-repeat` beside `order-captured`, and no new touch is logged. That ties it to money captured, not to the tap.

What it would answer: of the customers who repeat, how many do it through "lo de siempre", and whether those who use it churn less. The engine needs no change; it is one event type in the host config, one emit site, and a Clientes row.
<<<turn>>>
Yes, and that one is the cleanest of all, because both halves are already distinct counts on the same month document. With a `repeat-order-used` touch (customer owner, business dimension, emitted where the webhook accepts "lo de siempre"), a month document carries `distinct["repeat-order-used"]`, and it already carries `returned` (customers whose capture that month was not their first). Their ratio, read off one document, is "of the customers who repeated this month, how many used lo de siempre". It slots into Clientes beside Repiten as one more row, with no engine change.

Since the shortcut only exists after a first capture, it cannot contaminate the acquisition numbers, and the touch is what makes the other questions cheap:

1. Retention. Add it to `lifecycle.milestones` and the engine counts, among the month's new customers, none; but a second rule keyed on "reached the milestone before this month's capture" would split `returned` into repeaters who use it and repeaters who do not, so you can see whether the shortcut keeps people.
2. Adoption. `distinct["repeat-order-used"]` per month over `returned` per month on the 12 meses series shows the shortcut's share growing or not.
3. Per business. The same two numbers on each business row say where it is used.
4. Money. If the accepted order carries a flag, the order hooks can yield `order-captured-via-repeat` with the amounts, and Capturado splits by path.

The touch alone answers your question and 2 and 3. Retention needs the lifecycle rule, a small package change. Say the word when you want any of it as a backlog item.

noteText:
It seemsm like we manage issues with calls to db.* methods inconsistently. What is the best approach? Don't we have a "withNetworkIssue" (or something like that helper)?
<<<turn>>>
store
response:
Inconsistently is right. The stores that read Firestore (`useAttributionDocumentsStore`, `usePublicMenuStore`, the availability and location stores) wrap their reads in `withConnectivityHandling`, so a failed read resolves to a `ConnectivityError` carrying a `ConnectionStatus`, the offline banner rises, and a cached copy can be served. The three reads composables make directly through `db.*` on this branch do not: the Dashboard's spend read here, the spend list's read in `useCampaignSpendPage`, and the form's entry and label reads in `useCampaignSpendForm` each catch a raw error, set a `*Error` ref or report to Rollbar, and show their own message, so going offline on the spend screens looks like a broken read rather than an offline state.

Best approach: the same boundary for every read, which means either routing those three through a store that wraps them (a `useCampaignSpendStore`, matching how every other collection is read) or wrapping each direct read in `withConnectivityHandling` where it stands. The store is the shape the rest of hosting uses, and it would also give the spend list and the Campañas card one cached copy instead of two reads. Cost is a few hours. Which do you want?
<<<turn>>>
Done, commit 580aa2bd4 (docs in fde55e44c). `useCampaignSpendStore` now holds `entries`, `loading` and `error` the way `useAttributionDocumentsStore` does, clears on logout, and the three readers go through it: the Dashboard reads `spendStore.error` in the same chain as the documents store's errors, the spend page maps it to its retry message, and the form calls `loadForSource` and `loadEntry`, which throw so it can answer each failure itself. One correction to my earlier answer: `hosting/utils/db` was already built on `withConnectivityHandling`, so a failed spend read already raised the offline banner; what the composables lacked was the shared store and one error slot, which is what landed. Six older composables on main still read `db.*` directly (`useBusinessTermsPage`, `useBusinessSearch`, `useQRPage`, `usePendingQRConfigsPage`, `useOrderLocationRequirements`, `useSystemShutoffPage`); say so if you want a backlog item for them.

noteText:

response:
Took the first one, left the other two alone — here is what I found.

First, the thing that makes this decidable: taskName never reaches Cloud Tasks. createTaskEnqueuer only interpolates it into two logger.info lines ("Skipping X task enqueue in emulator" and "X task already exists, skipping"). It is a log label, nothing more.

So we had four vocabularies for five tasks, and they disagreed. Auto-cancel alone was TaskIdPrefix.AutoCancel = "autocancel", taskName "auto-cancel", and action "expire-unconfirmed-order" — three spellings of one task. Done: taskName now takes the GeneralTaskAction member in all five utilities, so the log says what the payload says and there is no free-floating string to keep in sync. Log output shifts accordingly ("auto-cancel task already exists" becomes "expire-unconfirmed-order task already exists"); nothing asserts on those strings and it is log-only, so there is no production risk. Commit 94f9b3674.

Renaming TaskIdPrefix to TaskName and reusing it for both — I would not. TaskIdPrefix is deliberately coarser than the action: EscalateLocation is shared by attempt 1 and attempt 2, because both belong to one chain keyed by location plus chain-start, with the attempt as a suffix. noteText: should this use the helper checkDocumentExists? This seems to be a common issue. Log to address at the retrospective.

No for this read, and the fact you had to ask is the actual defect — I left the reasoning out.

checkDocumentExists throws FunctionsInternalError when the document is missing. In a Cloud Task handler a throw is a retry signal: the general dispatcher runs retryConfig maxAttempts 3, so a genuinely missing order would be fetched and thrown on three times before Cloud Tasks gives up, and the order is never coming back. The plain get lets the handler log an error once and return, which ends the task cleanly.

noteText: why is this here?
response:
That line is firebase-kit logging, not the handler. FunctionsError's constructor calls logger.error itself — "Log errors so that they can trigger an alarm in the system" — so merely constructing the error emits a line before it is ever thrown. checkDocumentExists throws FunctionsInternalError when the doc is missing, so you get the kit's line first and my catch's line second.

[UNAUTHENTICATED] is not an auth failure. The kit appends it when the auth argument is undefined, which it always is here — task handlers run with no user, so every call site passes undefined. It reads alarming and means nothing.

Worth being straight about the cause: this pair is new, and it is from your previous note. Before I switched this read to checkDocumentExists it was a plain get with one specific "order location not found" log. The helper gives the consistency you asked for and costs a duplicate error line in a path we deliberately swallow. Both lines are error level, and per the taxonomy in functions/CLAUDE.md error is the level that raises an alert — which is right for a missing location, just twice.

Three ways to go, your call: leave it (consistent with the sibling handler, two lines per anomaly), go back to the plain get here for a single precise log, or push the fix upstream so the kit logs on throw rather than on construction. I would leave it and take the upstream fix if it ever bothers us in the console.

Three reasons it earns its place:

The whole of functions/src/* is declaration and routing, and every line of logic lives under utils/. fast.ts, app.ts, ai.ts and tasks/general.ts are all thin files that name secrets, set memory and timeouts, and dispatch. Inlining would put 248 lines of Firestore, Stripe and Slack work into the deploy manifest layer and make this the first exception to that rule.

It is also where the secrets get unwrapped. The wrapper calls .value() and hands the handler plain strings, exactly as tasks/general.ts does for its handlers. Inline it and .value() gets called from inside business logic, and the handler can no longer be driven with ordinary strings.

And the sizes make the point: 25 lines of config against 248 of logic. Merging them buys one fewer file and costs the separation.

Two things the split does not buy, to be straight about it. It is not isolating the handler for tests — handleCloseOutStaleOrders.test.ts drives closeOutStaleOrders.run(), so it goes through the wrapper anyway. And the small test that asserts the schedule and secret wiring only exists because the split exists. So the case rests on where logic lives, not on testing.

No change made. Say so if you would rather have it inlined and I will fold it in.

noteText:
Is this the only place we need to erad the order location just for a message? This seems like something we could just denormalize into the order?
<<<turn>>>

<<<turn>>>
unlisted is not that common. What would happen if we also cached unlisted? and added pickupGraceMinutes to the cached field list? Would that address all cases?

<<<turn>>>
auto-ready I expect to become a hot path. Why would you say this is not. Show me a list of one liners of what would be needed in order for the cache or perhaps an evolution on the cache to work?
<<<turn>>>
do the patch version
response:
Not the only place — three sites compute the pickup deadline, each reading the location doc first: this handler, handleInitiateOrderPayment.ts:297, and handleUpdateOrderStatus.ts:511 (the manual Lista path). So the pattern you are pointing at is real.

And the instinct fits the model: Order already denormalizes locationName, locationPhone, locationAddress, locationAddressNotes, locationGoogleMapsURL and businessName, each marked "(denormalized for performance)". Every one of those is a static display string, fixed when the order is created.

What these three reads actually need is a different kind of field. getPickupDeadline takes schedule, timeZone and pickupGraceMinutes, and computes against now — the deadline is the end of the current ordering window, not a stored value. schedule is live state staff edit through handleUpdateOrderLocationSchedule, and getPickupDeadline is deliberately built to read it live: its own doc says an accepted order keeps the schedule's pickup window even if the location paused after taking it, which is why it consults schedule but ignores status. Snapshot the schedule onto the order at creation and a business that fixes its hours mid-order would have customers told a deadline from the old hours, with nothing to signal the drift. timeZone on its own is effectively immutable and safe to copy, but copying only that does not remove the read, since schedule still has to come from somewhere.

If the goal is fewer reads rather than fewer fields, the lever already exists: getCachedOrderLocations caches schedule and timeZone for two minutes and discovery uses it. Pointing the three deadline sites at that would cut the reads without moving live state onto the order — at the cost of a deadline up to two minutes stale, which for an end-of-window time is probably fine.

Want me to write it up as a backlog item — and if so, the cache route or denormalizing timeZone plus a schedule snapshot?

Stopped before writing it, because I checked the cache properly this time and my recommendation was built on an incomplete read. Two things I missed:

1. The cache only holds discoverable locations, and discoverable is [Enabled, Paused]. Orderable is [Enabled, Unlisted]. So an Unlisted location — one that takes orders by direct link and is deliberately absent from search — is never in the cache. Route the deadline reads through it and every order at an Unlisted location misses, and a Disabled one too.
2. The cache selects a fixed field list that has schedule and timeZone but not pickupGraceMinutes. getPickupDeadline takes all three, so any location with a custom grace would silently fall back to the default and get the wrong deadline.

And the third site cannot use it at all. handleInitiateOrderPayment needs slug (not cached) and gates on isLocationOrderable, which is exactly the Unlisted case the cache excludes. It reads the location for six other reasons; the deadline is incidental.

So the honest version of the cache route is: add pickupGraceMinutes to the cached field list, add a by-id helper that falls back to a direct read on a miss, and use it at two of the three sites — the mark-ready path and the auto-ready task. That saves one read per mark-ready and per auto-ready fire, still reads directly for Unlisted and Disabled, and puts a cache built for discovery into the notification path.

My recommendation flipped: I would not do it. The gain is two reads on low-frequency paths, against a new helper, a widened cache, and a fallback branch that has to stay correct. I would rather leave three direct reads that are obviously right. I was wrong to call this the real option before checking the status sets.

Say the word if you still want it and I will build the fallback version — I just did not want to ship it on a premise that turned out to be wrong.
<<<turn>>>
pickupGraceMinutes is trivial — one entry in the field list. Caching Unlisted is not, and here is the thing that decides it: the cache query is the only status filter in the whole discovery path. I checked the two consumers and neither filters status. getVisibleOrderLocations only filters on test access. searchOrderLocations does not look at status at all.

So the moment Unlisted enters the cache it enters customer-facing search: the restaurant list in handleMessage, restaurant discovery, the freeform-text search paths, and repeat-order routing. That is the one thing Unlisted exists to prevent — the config page literally describes it as not appearing in search but still taking orders by direct link. It would also need the same change in applyIncrementalUpdates, which currently evicts anything not discoverable.

You can have it, but the safe version is: add Unlisted to the cache, then add a status filter to getVisibleOrderLocations and searchOrderLocations so it stays out of search. That is discovery code on the highest-traffic path in the system — every inbound message — being changed to serve two low-frequency notification reads.

And it still would not address all cases. Two left over:

1. Disabled. Staff can disable a location that has live paid orders — that is the premise of the existing backlog item about cancelling unpaid orders when a location is paused or disabled, which leaves paid ones alone. Such an order still needs mark-ready and auto-ready, and Disabled would not be in the cache.
2. handleInitiateOrderPayment still cannot use it. It needs slug, which is not cached, and it gates on isLocationOrderable, so it reads the doc for six other reasons regardless.

Which means you would still want a fallback read on a miss, and one of the three sites never uses the cache at all.

If you want the cache to actually cover this, the coherent end state is different: make it cache every order location and move status filtering into the consumers, so it stops being "the discoverable ones" and becomes "the locations". That is defensible and probably better long term, but it is a discovery-layer refactor with its own testing, not something to bolt onto this branch.

My recommendation is unchanged: leave the three direct reads. If you want the refactor I will write it up as a backlog item with this analysis in it.
<<<turn>>>
You are right and I was wrong to call it low-frequency. I was thinking per-site rather than per-order. Counting the location doc reads across one order lifecycle: payment init reads it, the accept branch reads it again for the preparation minutes, and then either mark-ready or auto-ready reads it a third time. Three reads of the same document per order, scaling with order volume — and auto-ready makes the third one automatic rather than dependent on staff tapping anything. That is worth fixing.

What it would take, using the cache as it stands:

1. Add pickupGraceMinutes to OrderLocationFieldList — getPickupDeadline takes it and it is not cached today, so deadlines would silently use the default.
2. Add slug to the same list — the only field handleInitiateOrderPayment needs that the cache lacks.
3. Add Unlisted to the cached status set, since the cache query is discoverableQuery (Enabled + Paused) and Unlisted takes orders.
4. Add a status filter to getVisibleOrderLocations, which today filters only on test access.
5. Add a status filter to searchOrderLocations, which today filters on nothing — it feeds restaurant discovery, two freeform-text paths, and repeat-order routing.
6. Update the eviction check in applyIncrementalUpdates, which drops anything outside DiscoverableOrderLocationStatuses on every incremental refresh.
7. Add a by-id lookup helper — consumers get an array today, and these three sites want one location by id.
8. Fall back to a direct read on a miss, because Disabled is still never cached and a paid order survives its location being disabled.
9. Reconcile the shape: CachedOrderLocation renames name to locationName and adds orderLocationId, so either the helper returns something OrderLocation-shaped or all three call sites adapt.
10. Accept up to two minutes of schedule staleness in the pickup deadline, and decide that is fine — it is an end-of-window time, so it almost always is, but it is a real semantic change.

The evolution version, which I think is the better shape:

11. Cache every order location instead of only the discoverable ones — drop discoverableQuery, keep status as data rather than a filter baked into the cache.
12. Move every status decision into the consumers, which is items 4 and 5 anyway.
13. Then the by-id helper serves all three sites with no fallback branch, because every location is present — item 8 disappears.
14. Still needs items 1, 2, 6, 9 and 10.
15. Accept that the cache now holds Disabled locations too, which grows with churn rather than with active restaurants — negligible at this scale, worth saying out loud.

So the evolution is roughly the same work as the patch, minus the fallback branch, and it leaves a cache whose name matches what it holds. If you want it, I would do it as its own change rather than inside this branch — it touches the highest-traffic path in the system and wants its own testing — but I am happy to start it now if you would rather not context-switch.
<<<turn>>>
Done, with one deliberate subtraction I want to flag up front: I did not convert handleInitiateOrderPayment, and I dropped slug from the cache because that site was its only reason to exist. Reason below.

What landed (commit 2b05d9fcd):

CachedOrderLocationStatuses is a new constant, Enabled + Paused + Unlisted, and orderLocationRefs.discoverableQuery became cacheableQuery against it. applyIncrementalUpdates evicts on the same set. pickupGraceMinutes joined the cached field list, so deadlines no longer silently fall back to the default.

getVisibleOrderLocations now filters to DiscoverableOrderLocationStatuses. That is the whole behavior-preservation story: searchOrderLocations goes through it, so one filter keeps unlisted locations out of the restaurant list, discovery, both freeform-text paths and repeat routing. I added a test for it and mutation-checked it — dropping the filter fails that test and only that test.

getCachedOrderLocationById is the by-id helper, cache first and a document read on a miss. The field list and the doc-to-cached mapper moved to internal/cachedOrderLocationFields.ts so both paths build the identical shape; the mapper now assigns fields explicitly rather than spreading, so a select-ed query and a full doc read cannot drift.

Wired at the two deadline sites: handleAutoReadyOrder and the mark-ready branch of handleUpdateOrderStatus.

Now the subtraction. handleInitiateOrderPayment does not just read the location for the deadline — it gates on isLocationOrderable(orderLocation) before creating a checkout session. Behind a two-minute cache that means a location staff just paused or disabled keeps accepting payments for up to two minutes. Extracted the part that is genuinely shared, and deliberately not the transaction. Commit 4a646c3cc.

What I compared: the sweep block here against the PickedUp case in handleUpdateOrderStatus.ts. The overlap is the capture field set — capturedAt falling back to now, capturedDate through getDateInPRTimeZone, and stripeCapture reduced to chargeId and balanceTransactionId. The callable stamps by: authData.uid; the sweep omits by, which is the system-attribution convention. A shared helper would need parameters for the guard, the actor, the missing-document behaviour and the return shape — a config object with branches, and both callers would still read differently. Evidence the extraction is behaviour-preserving: 223 tests across order-payment, scheduled, callable/fast and src/scheduled pass with no snapshot changes at either call site.

The helper got a colocated test, and my first version of it passed a mutation it should have failed — I set the capture timestamp to the same instant as the fake clock, so using the capture time and using the write time produced identical output. The test proved nothing. Fixed the fixtures to sit on different days: one capture a day before the clock, one at 2025-01-20T02:30Z which is 2025-01-19 in PR, so UTC conversion and write-time fallback both produce a wrong answer. noteText: Thre seems to be a type issue here
response:
I cannot reproduce an error on that line, so I want to check what you are seeing before changing anything. npx tsc --noEmit -p functions/tsconfig.json exits 0 with no output, and yarn build-tsc reports nothing for this file.

Why it compiles: data is DBOrderLocation, and the parameter is OrderLocationFields, which is Pick<DBOrderLocation, ...>. A wider object is assignable to a narrower structural type, and excess-property checking only applies to fresh object literals, which this is not. So handing the mapper a complete document is legal and it reads only the picked fields.

That said, looking at it next to the other two call sites did turn up something worth your eye, and it is the opposite of what the note points at. In getCachedOrderLocations the value is doc.data() as OrderLocationFields, at lines 36 and 57. Those are assertions, not inferences: .select() returns only the selected fields at runtime while Firestore still types .data() as the whole document, so the cast tells the compiler something it cannot check. It is sound today only because the same OrderLocationFieldList feeds both .select(...) and the Pick, so the two cannot drift. Line 31 here is the one place with no cast, because the document really is complete.

So: is the thing you spotted the cast pair rather than this line? Or is your editor showing a diagnostic mine is not — if so, paste it and I will chase it, since a stale TS server after the constants/types split is plausible.

noteText:
What is this about? Why is this special?
<<<turn>>>
Is there something we can do in firebase-kit-client so that this special entry is not needed?
response:
Explanation only, no change. Vitest externalizes packages whose real path is inside node_modules: their imports run natively and bypass vitest's module registry. While firebase-kit-* were workspace symlinks (realpath under packages/) vitest processed them, so the suite's vi.mock('firebase-functions') / vi.mock('firebase-admin/*') calls intercepted the imports the kit makes internally (e.g. checkClaimsVersion → getAuth, parseCallableRequest → firebase-functions). Installed from npm they'd be externalized and those mocks would silently stop applying inside the kit — tests would hit the real modules. server.deps.inline forces vitest to keep processing these two packages, preserving the exact pre-migration module graph. Task 2.1 proved it load-bearing by removal: without the hosting entry the suite fails with 'indexedDB is not defined' (getsetdel's own idb-keyval import escapes the mock). Same mechanism firebase-kit-client documents in its own vitest config for getsetdel.
<<<turn>>>
Not cleanly from the package side today: externalization is vitest's own node_modules policy and it offers no package-side opt-out flag — the consumer-config inline entry is the ecosystem-standard answer (getsetdel's README documents the identical requirement for itself). The real package-side fix is an API change: have the kit accept its firebase collaborators as injected dependencies so consumer tests never need vi.mock to reach inside it — createActionableFunctionCaller already optionally takes dependencies.functions, so the pattern half-exists. That's an ericvera/firebase-kit change, not this branch, so I filed it per the out-of-scope rule: Todoist 6hJH7xHG2F5MVJrF '[spike] evaluate a firebase-kit API to drop the vitest server.deps.inline requirement in consumers' (Okven - R&D → To Do).

Task 2.1 proved it load-bearing by removal: without the hosting entry the suite fails with 'indexedDB is not defined' (getsetdel's own idb-keyval import escapes the mock). Same mechanism firebase-kit-client documents in its own vitest config for getsetdel.
<<<turn>>>
Not cleanly from the package side today: externalization is vitest's own node_modules policy and it offers no package-side opt-out flag — the consumer-config inline entry is the ecosystem-standard answer (getsetdel's README documents the identical requirement for itself). The real package-side fix is an API change: have the kit accept its firebase collaborators as injected dependencies so consumer tests never need vi.mock to reach inside it — createActionableFunctionCaller already optionally takes dependencies.functions, so the pattern half-exists. That's an ericvera/firebase-kit change, not this branch, so I filed it per the out-of-scope rule: Todoist 6hJH7xHG2F5MVJrF '[spike] evaluate a firebase-kit API to drop the vitest server.deps.inline requirement in consumers' (Okven - R&D → To Do).
